questions.q: Why does Meridian qualify for Domain Separation under Chapter 2's actual test, rather than it being a default choice for any multi-department organization?
options: St. Catherine's, Lakeshore, and Prairie View function like genuinely separate subsidiaries under one new parent, with a real need to keep day-to-day data apart while corporate still needs a combined view
The three hospital systems asked for separate instances and Domain Separation was offered as a compromise
ServiceNow technically cannot run HR Service Delivery without Domain Separation enabled
Domain Separation is required any time an organization has more than one physical location
questions.explain: Chapter 2 named two legitimate use cases for Domain Separation — separate subsidiaries under one parent, or an MSP's distinct clients. Meridian's structure matches the first one precisely.

questions.q: Why does this lesson choose a 'system of engagement vs. system of record' approach instead of migrating all three legacy HR systems onto one platform immediately?
options: Workday, ADP, and PeopleSoft all use an identical API, so no real integration work is needed
ServiceNow HR Service Delivery cannot integrate with more than one external HR system at a time
Legacy HR migrations are never part of a Technical Architect's responsibility

A full migration of Workday, ADP, and the Prairie View PeopleSoft module within an 18-month window is unrealistic, so ServiceNow becomes where HR work happens while each legacy system stays the record of truth for now
questions.explain: The capstone explicitly avoids forcing an unrealistic big-bang HR migration, choosing a phased integration architecture instead.

questions.q: Why is a new-hire record syncing from Workday into ServiceNow a good fit for event-driven integration, per Chapter 4's criteria?
options: Nobody is waiting on that sync to continue a user-facing transaction, so the publishing system doesn't need to wait for an immediate response
Workday cannot technically support request-response integration
Event-driven integration is always more secure than request-response, regardless of the data involved
New-hire records change so rarely that no integration pattern actually matters here
questions.explain: Chapter 4's test for event-driven integration is exactly this: no one needs an immediate answer to continue, so asynchronous processing avoids unnecessary coupling.

questions.q: Why does this lesson apply strict, audited access only to a narrow set of regulated tables and fields, rather than locking down the entire platform uniformly?
options: Uniform restriction is actually cheaper to configure than targeted restriction
Lakeshore and Prairie View staff requested that all security controls be removed
Chapter 5's security-usability lesson shows that uniform maximum restriction drives users toward shared logins or shadow trackers — risk-proportionate friction avoids manufacturing that outcome
Regulated healthcare data does not require any special access controls under HIPAA
questions.explain: This directly applies Chapter 5's risk-proportionate friction principle to avoid the workaround failure mode it describes.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say domain separation, the integration architecture, and the security design all have to reinforce each other rather than being treated as three separate decisions?
options: Incoming HR records must be tagged to the correct domain or domain separation breaks silently, and the Meridian corporate domain — where data crosses hospital boundaries — is exactly where the strictest security controls matter most
ServiceNow requires all three features to be configured in the same change request
There is no real connection between domain separation, integrations, and security architecture
Security architecture only applies to the top-level domain and nowhere else
questions.explain: The lesson shows these three decisions lock together: integrations must respect domain structure, and the domain structure defines where security risk concentrates.
